steps.text:
Why a routine at all. Your games say your tactical eye is fine: when the best move is a capture or a check, you find it about 87% of the time. What goes missing is the moment of looking. Pieces get left where they can be taken, and you spend more time on those moves than on ordinary ones, not less.

So the fix is not more calculation. It is two short looks that happen on every move, whether or not anything is there.

The blitz version: two looks.

  • Look 1, when they move: what of mine can they take right now? If their move was a check, what else does the checking piece attack?
  • Look 2, move chosen, hand not yet moved: lands, leaves. Where does my piece land and what can take it there? What was it guarding or blocking?

That is all that fits in 3+2. Count attackers and defenders only when a piece is attacked and both looks otherwise come up clean.

Look 1, in one of your games.

They have just played d4.

Before you choose a move, Look 1: what can they take right now? Bxg5 would take the queen on g5 for nothing.
You played cxd4 instead, and they took it. About four in ten of the pieces you lose this way are like this one. Nothing needed picturing: the capture was on the board as it stood.

Look 2, lands.

You played Nc6 (blue arrow).

Lands: the knight on c6 can be taken where it stands: Nxc6 takes the knight on c6 for nothing.

Leaves: nothing it was guarding or blocking is now short.

Look 2, leaves.

You played Qf3 (blue arrow).

Lands: nothing can capture on f3.

Leaves: it was guarding the rook on a1, and now Qxa1+ takes the rook on a1 for nothing.

The slow version: four steps. For correspondence games, cards, and any game with real time.

  1. Their move. What does it attack now? What did it stop guarding, or unblock? Then: if they moved again right now, what would they do?
  2. Inventory. Which of my pieces are loose (undefended, or attacked by something cheaper)? Which of theirs?
  3. Candidates. My checks, captures and threats first, then quiet moves. No idea at all: improve the worst-placed piece. Ahead in material: trade pieces, not pawns.
  4. Safety check on the move chosen, before playing it: lands, leaves, then their checks and captures in the new position. If something fails, back to step 3.

The two looks are steps 1 and 4 with everything else squeezed out.

What a threat is. A threat is a quiet move (no capture, no check) that sets up a capture or a mate on the move after. The practical question is the one in step 1: if they moved twice in a row, what would they do?

A typical middlegame position of yours has about three such ideas for the opponent, and one in ten has eight or more. So do not try to list them. Find the biggest one.

The common kind: the same piece moves twice. In about 86% of two-move ideas the piece that moves first is also the piece that captures. You already picture these.

Gold arrow: the quiet first move, d4. Red arrow: what it sets up. Then dxc3 wins the knight.

The kind you said you cannot picture: a different piece captures. One piece steps aside, or drives a guard away, and another piece takes. It is about one idea in seven.

Gold arrow: the quiet first move, Rh6. Red arrow: what it sets up. Then Qh1# is mate. A different piece does the capturing: the first move only cleared the way or removed a guard.

How the decks fit together.

  • Anatomy of a hang: your own lost pieces taken apart by cause. Read these first.
  • Walkthroughs: the whole routine run move after move on three stretches of your games.
  • S1 to S3: warm-ups. Checks, captures, loose pieces, on the board as it stands.
  • S4: lands and leaves, with the move named but not shown.
  • S5: two moves in a row, biggest threat only. S5b is the different-piece kind.
  • S6: the two looks on four to six consecutive moves of a real game. This is the one that replaces the old play-forward cards.

Every answer key in these decks is worked out from the rules alone: legal moves, what attacks what, and who comes out ahead if everything trades on a square. No engine. The cost: a capture the key calls winning is occasionally a bad idea for a reason the count cannot see (a pin, a counter-threat). Each answer has an I think the key is wrong button for that.

cards.t: The two looks and the four steps
